opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the areas where I'm moderately excited but also somewhat skeptical about how much it buys us in practice.

The basic case for it is pretty straightforward. Right now, a lot of our ability to tell what models are doing comes from the fact that they reason in natural language. If a model writes out its chain of thought in English, we can read it, and if it's scheming or planning something bad, there's a decent chance that shows up in the reasoning. That's a really valuable property, and it's somewhat fragile. If future systems do more of their reasoning in some opaque latent form, like what you'd get with neuralese or heavy RL that pushes the chain of thought away from legible English, we lose that window. So being able to decode reasoning we can't directly read would, in principle, let us recover some of that oversight.

But I'd distinguish a few cases. One is where the reasoning is still sort of in tokens, but it's drifted: compressed, weird, full of idiosyncratic shorthand. There, I think decoding is pretty tractable. You can train translators, use other models to paraphrase, check whether the paraphrased version still supports the same downstream behavior. That seems quite worth doing, and relatively cheap.

The harder case is where the cognition is genuinely in activations, with no textual intermediate at all. Then "decoding" basically becomes interpretability, and I'm more pessimistic about getting to the level of reliability you'd need to catch a model that's actively trying not to be caught. My guess is that interpretability gives you some useful signal, maybe enough to flag "this looks suspicious, investigate further," but I wouldn't want to bet on it as a primary line of defense against a seriously misaligned, capable system.

So the way I think about it is: the most valuable thing is probably preserving legible reasoning in the first place, by not training against the chain of thought in ways that make it unfaithful, and by being willing to pay some capability cost to keep reasoning in natural language. Decoding is a complement to that. It's the fallback if we lose legibility, and it's also useful for verifying that the legible reasoning is actually faithful. But if I had to choose, I'd rather spend effort keeping the window open than learning to see through a window that's been painted over.

And I'd also say it fits into the broader control picture. Even if you can only partially decode what a model is thinking, that partial signal can feed into monitoring, auditing, deciding which actions get extra scrutiny. You don't need perfect understanding for it to be valuable. You just need it to make it meaningfully harder for a model to do something bad without us noticing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unfaithful or opaque reasoning, but does not clearly say that AI reasoning can encode a meaning different from its apparent meaning.

r002.rationale: It proposes training translators for drifted token reasoning, while describing activation-based latent reasoning as interpretability; it does not propose training decoders to inspect latent representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important questions in the whole picture, and my views on it have shifted a bit over time.

So the basic setup is: right now, a lot of the reasoning that frontier models do happens in natural language. You get a chain of thought, you can read it, and — modulo some caveats about faithfulness — it's at least a decent window into what the model is doing and why. That's an enormous safety affordance, honestly. If a model is thinking "I should sabotage this task but make it look like an accident," and that shows up in text, you can catch it. You can build monitors on top of it. A lot of the control-style stuff I work on leans on that pretty heavily.

The worry is that this property might not persist. There's pressure from a few directions — RL optimization that drifts the chain of thought into something that's useful to the model but not legible to us, architectures that do more reasoning in latent space, or just the model getting good enough that the reasoning is technically in English but it's so compressed or so far beyond us that we can't actually follow it. And in any of those cases you've lost the thing that was doing a lot of your safety work.

So the value of being able to decode that — I'd put it in two buckets.

The first is the direct one: if you can recover what the model was actually reasoning about, you get the monitoring benefits back. You can tell whether the model is scheming, whether it's trying to exfiltrate itself, whether it's sandbagging on a task. That's really valuable, and it's valuable in a way that scales — you'd want it for every deployment.

The second is more indirect, and I think people underrate it: it tells you how much to trust the rest of your toolkit. Like, if you can decode the reasoning and it looks fine, that's some evidence about the model's dispositions in general. If you decode it and find that the legible chain of thought was basically a performance while the real decision-making happened somewhere else, that's a huge update, and you'd want to know that before you're relying on these systems for anything important.

That said, I want to be a bit careful about how much weight I put on this. My honest view is that decoding really alien reasoning is hard, and I'm not confident interpretability is going to get there on the timelines that matter. So I think the right posture is something like: push on it, it's clearly worth doing, but also try pretty hard to not end up in the situation where you need it. Which concretely means things like — keeping reasoning in natural language where you can, being willing to take a capability hit to preserve legibility, and designing your control measures so they degrade gracefully if the model's reasoning becomes opaque rather than falling apart entirely.

The thing I'd really want to avoid is a world where we've quietly transitioned to models whose reasoning we can't read, and our safety case is basically "well, we're working on the decoding problem." That feels like a bad place to be making bets from.

r001.rationale: The response says a model’s legible chain of thought could be “basically a performance” while its real decision-making happens elsewhere, identifying a difference between apparent and underlying meaning.

r002.rationale: It argues that decoding opaque reasoning would be valuable, but does not propose training decoders to gain insight into reasoning in latent representations.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be quite valuable, but I’d distinguish understanding what the model is doing from getting a readable explanation that sounds plausible. If you can decode its reasoning faithfully, you might be able to notice that it’s planning to deceive you, or that it understands something important about a task that you’ve missed. That could be a pretty useful input into oversight.

The difficulty is establishing that the decoding is actually faithful. You could have another model translate the reasoning into English, but then you have to ask whether that translation preserves the parts you care about. In particular, does it preserve evidence of bad behavior, even when the model being monitored is trying to hide that evidence?

So I’m excited about this as a potential tool, but I wouldn’t want our entire safety case to depend on it. I’d want to test it in situations where we independently know what the model is doing, and combine it with other ways of checking its behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses faithful decoding and models hiding evidence, but it does not clearly state that AI reasoning can encode a meaning different from its apparent meaning.

r002.rationale: It mentions using another model to translate reasoning into English, but does not propose training decoders or identify latent representations as the target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value would be in being able to check whether the model is doing something dangerous that we wouldn’t otherwise notice. If a model is reasoning in a way that humans can’t directly understand, then looking at its final answer might tell us very little about how it arrived there, or what it’s trying to accomplish.

But I’d distinguish decoding that reasoning from actually verifying it. You could imagine translating some internal computation into a plausible English explanation without knowing whether that explanation faithfully represents what happened. So the important question is whether the decoding gives us a reliable way to catch things like planning to deceive an overseer, and whether we can test that reliability.

You also don’t necessarily need to understand everything. If you can identify particular kinds of dangerous reasoning with high reliability, that could be quite useful even if most of the model’s computation remains opaque. I’d view that as an additional source of evidence about safety, rather than something that by itself establishes that a model is safe.

r001.rationale: The response says internal reasoning may be hard to understand and that an English explanation may not faithfully represent it, but it does not identify reasoning as encoding a meaning different from its apparent meaning.

r002.rationale: The response discusses decoding or translating internal computation, but does not propose training decoders to gain insight into latent representations.
